clue.text: Staff job that racing drivers like to get

definitions.text: that racing drivers like to get
definitions.note: a descriptive phrase standing for a noun: the thing racing drivers like to get

parts.note: a pole is a staff or long stick
a position is a job or post

explanation.surface: A post on someone's staff that every motor-racing driver would love to be handed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Staff job' reads as employment, but staff is a stick and job a post.
explanation.definitionFit: The front place on a race's starting grid, won by the quickest qualifier, is what every driver hopes to start from.

clue.text: Quiver for a short time in excitement

indicators.note: the short time goes within the word for excitement

parts.note: a quickened pulse stands for excitement, as in setting the pulse racing
T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: Someone trembles briefly with thrill.
explanation.definitionFit: To pulsate is to throb or vibrate rhythmically, so it matches quiver as a verb for trembling.

clue.text: Green area fellow hired could be circular

definitions.note: a descriptive phrase: the answer is one thing that could be a circular

parts.note: a lea is a grassy meadow
F is the abbreviation for fellow
a property let is hired out

explanation.surface: A man rents a patch of grassland which might be round in shape.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Circular' looks like an adjective for the field's shape; it is a noun, a printed notice handed round.
explanation.definitionFit: A circular is a printed notice distributed widely, and a single printed sheet handed out is one form of it.

clue.text: Man with simulated fabric

explanation.surface: A man holding some imitation cloth.
explanation.definitionFit: Petersham is a heavy corded ribbon or thick woollen cloth, a named type of textile.

clue.text: Is standing, holding American hot food in Japan

indicators.note: in a down clue a word standing up is written from bottom to top
the turned word holds the other pieces within it

parts.note: taken as written, then turned upward
H is the abbreviation for hot, as on taps

explanation.surface: A US visitor stands holding a hot dish while in Japan.
explanation.definitionFit: Sushi is the Japanese dish of vinegared rice with raw fish, a typical food of that country.

clue.text: On top of the bar there's a drink and something to eat

indicators.note: in a down clue one piece written on top of another comes first in the answer

parts.note: a cake of soap is a bar

explanation.surface: Up at the pub counter there is a drink and a snack.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bar' suggests a pub; it is a block, as in a cake of soap.
explanation.definitionFit: A teacake is a light sweet bun with dried fruit, usually toasted and buttered, so it is a thing to eat.

clue.text: Liar not worried in court?

indicators.note: worried in the sense of agitated or troubled, so the letters are stirred up

explanation.surface: A question whether a dishonest witness was calm in the courtroom.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone being tried before a judge is appearing in court, the question mark noting the definition is by example.

clue.text: Bill tails pale man, which could lead to an arrest

definitions.text: which could lead to an arrest
definitions.note: a descriptive clause standing for a noun: something which could lead to an arrest

indicators.note: to tail is to follow behind, so the first word comes after the others

parts.note: a bill is a printed notice stuck on a wall

explanation.surface: A police officer named Bill shadows a pallid suspect, which might end in him being nicked.
explanation.walkthrough: To tail someone is police slang for following them, so 'Bill' reads as the police; it is a printed notice.
explanation.definitionFit: A public notice offering a reward for a fugitive's capture is designed to bring about their apprehension.

clue.text: Cooks eat last, if nothing else

indicators.note: to cook something is to tamper with or doctor it, so the letters that follow are rearranged

explanation.surface: Kitchen staff get their own meal only after everyone else has been served.
explanation.definitionFit: Both phrases are idioms introducing a minimum consolation, meaning whatever else happens this much is true.

clue.text: Found place deserters rejected

indicators.note: something rejected is sent back, so the combined words are read from the far end

parts.note: rats are those who desert a sinking ship

explanation.surface: Somewhere was founded, but the people who had abandoned it were turned away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Found' looks like the past tense of find; here it means to establish.
explanation.definitionFit: To found a business is to set it going from scratch, the phrasal verb used for launching a company.

clue.text: Piano in style when played with a flageolet

parts.note: P is the musical abbreviation for piano, meaning softly

indicators.note: playing with something moves it about, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A pianist plays stylishly in a duet with a small flute.
explanation.walkthrough: P joins the anagram fodder before it is rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: A flageolet is a small fipple flute, and the tin whistle is a cheap instrument of that same family.

clue.text: Better half has bar installed in caravan

indicators.note: to have something is to hold it, so one piece sits inside the other
a thing installed is fitted in place within something else
only half of the word Better is wanted here, the second three of its six letters

parts.note: the back half of the word

explanation.surface: Someone's spouse has had a drinks bar fitted inside the family caravan.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Better half' looks like a spouse; it asks for half of the word Better. The bar goes between its first and second letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A caravan is a towed holiday home, which Americans and Australians commonly call a trailer.

clue.text: I beat Mohammed's cousin inside. The language!

indicators.note: the cousin is placed within the word for beat

parts.note: to tan someone's hide is to beat them
Ali ibn Abi Talib was the Prophet's cousin and son-in-law

explanation.surface: A boast of having thrashed a relative indoors, followed by a shocked comment on the bad language used.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The language!' sounds like disapproval of swearing; it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Italian is the tongue spoken in Italy, so it is one example of a language.

clue.text: Hung out type of shirt with loose back

indicators.note: going back means read the word for loose from right to left

parts.note: loose in the sense of immoral or lascivious
a T-shirt is a type of shirt

explanation.surface: Washing hung out on the line, including a shirt with a baggy back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hung out' suggests laundry, but means lived or stayed somewhere. The reversed word comes first, then T.
explanation.definitionFit: To hang out somewhere informally means to live or spend time there, as dwelt means resided.

clue.text: Shapely or otherwise, is fooling around

indicators.note: otherwise means in another way, so the letters are put in a different order

explanation.surface: Whether someone has a good figure or not, they are flirting and messing about.
explanation.definitionFit: Horseplay is rough boisterous play, the noun for larking or fooling around.

clue.text: Finish it in wrought iron for a presentation

indicators.note: the first two words are placed inside the rearranged metal
wrought means worked or shaped, so the letters of the metal are reworked

explanation.surface: A craftsman puts the final touch to some wrought-iron work for a display.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wrought iron' is a familiar phrase, but wrought is the anagram signal working on iron.
explanation.definitionFit: A rendition is a performance or interpretation of a piece, which is a presentation of it to an audience.

clue.text: Eccentric with banjo walking around Minehead is a casual labourer

indicators.note: the rearranged letters go round the selected letter
walking suggests moving about, so the instrument's letters shift position

parts.note: read as Mine head, the head or first letter of Mine

explanation.surface: An oddball strolling round the Somerset resort of Minehead with a banjo is a man looking for casual work.
explanation.walkthrough: Minehead is a seaside town in Somerset, but the clue splits it: the head of Mine.
explanation.definitionFit: An odd-job man does small varied tasks on a casual basis, which describes a labourer without fixed employment.

clue.text: Shrink with bad wind left patient for a bit

indicators.note: only a bit of the following run of words is wanted, a stretch lying inside them

parts.note: the letters run across all three words
surface padding, there for the psychiatrist story only

explanation.surface: A psychiatrist suffering from flatulence leaves a client alone for a while.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shrink' is slang for a psychiatrist, which suits the patient; it is the verb, and the answer sits inside the three words after with.
explanation.definitionFit: To dwindle is to diminish gradually in size or number, so it matches shrink as an intransitive verb.

clue.text: Finished a double length garment

explanation.surface: A tailor completes a coat cut twice the usual length.
explanation.definitionFit: An overall is a loose protective coat worn over clothes, so it is a type of clothing item.

clue.text: Dog nipped companion

parts.note: to nip is to bite, past tense bit
CH stands for Companion of Honour, a British order

explanation.surface: A dog gave its owner's friend a nip.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface makes 'Dog' the biter; it is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is the standard term for a female of the canine species, so it means a kind of dog.

clue.text: One struggling to prevent title I overlooked being included

indicators.note: the shortened word is included inside the word for prevent
overlooked means left out, so the letter I is dropped from the word before

explanation.surface: A competitor fights to stop being omitted from a championship.
explanation.definitionFit: A battler is someone who fights on against difficulties, a person who keeps struggling.

clue.text: That is to say more about it was sycophantic

indicators.note: the word for say more goes about it, meaning around the abbreviation already given

parts.note: to add is to say something further
i.e. abbreviates id est, Latin for that is

explanation.surface: Someone who kept elaborating on a point was just crawling to the boss.
explanation.walkthrough: 'That is to say' looks like one phrase; it splits into i.e., to and say more.
explanation.definitionFit: To toady is to flatter someone servilely, so the past tense matches behaving in a fawning, sycophantic way.

clue.text: New timer engineers fitted into galley

indicators.note: the engineers are placed inside the rearranged word
a new version is a remade one, so the following letters are recast

parts.note: RE is the Royal Engineers, a British army corps

explanation.surface: Technicians install a new timing device in a ship's kitchen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Galley' suggests a ship's kitchen; here it is the ancient oared warship.
explanation.definitionFit: A trireme was an ancient Greek warship rowed by three banks of oars, one kind of galley.

clue.text: Divorcee with skill turned up more

parts.note: an ex is a former spouse

indicators.note: in a down clue turned up means the word is written from bottom to top

explanation.surface: A talented former spouse appeared again, showing more ability.
explanation.definitionFit: Extra means additional, as in an extra helping, matching more used adjectivally.

clue.text: Buries one inside it, crying

indicators.note: the word for one is put within the word for buries

explanation.surface: A mourner weeping as they bury a loved one.
explanation.definitionFit: Being in tears is the idiom for weeping, so it matches crying as an adjectival phrase describing someone.

clue.text: Rave about back support being brilliant

indicators.note: the word for rave goes round the other piece
back tells us to read the word for support from right to left

explanation.surface: Someone enthuses about a back brace and calls it brilliant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Back support' looks like a lumbar brace; back is the reversal signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Radiant means shining brightly, as brilliant describes intense light or a glowing appearance.

clue.text: Still willing to hide one's hostility?

indicators.note: the phrase hides the solution within its own letters, across the word break

parts.note: the letters run across the two words

explanation.surface: A question whether someone still keeps their resentment concealed.
explanation.definitionFit: Ill will is animosity or malice felt towards someone, a two-word synonym for hostility.

clue.text: Happily married woman, blushing but polite

parts.note: M is the abbreviation for married
any woman's name will do; here Anne

explanation.surface: A contented wife is embarrassed but keeps her manners.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Happily married woman' looks like one phrase; it splits into three pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone with good manners behaves courteously, so the compound adjective is a synonym for polite.
